interview.a: The one-time code is exchanged server-side with the client secret, so tokens are never exposed in the browser URL and a stolen code alone is useless.

interview.q: How does TOTP work?
interview.a: Both the server and authenticator app share a secret and compute a 6-digit code from the secret and the current 30-second time window; the server recomputes and compares it.

topics.title: Email Verification and Password Reset Flow
topics.summary: Use single-use, expiring, hashed tokens sent by email to verify addresses and reset passwords securely.
topics.description:
Both features use the same pattern: **prove control of an email address** with a secret link.

### Token design
1. Generate a random token: `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')`.
2. Email the raw token in a link: `https://app.com/reset-password?token=...`.
3. Store only a **hash** of the token (`sha256`) plus an **expiry** (10-60 min) in the database. If the DB leaks, the links are useless.
4. When the user opens the link, hash the incoming token, find a user with that hash and a non-expired date.
5. Perform the action, then **delete the token** (single use).

### Email verification
After registration set `isVerified: false` and email a verify link. `GET /auth/verify-email?token=...` sets `isVerified: true`. Block login (or sensitive actions) until verified, and allow re-sending (rate-limited).

### Password reset
1. `POST /auth/forgot-password { email }` - **always** respond `200` with "If that email exists, we sent a link" so you do not reveal which emails are registered.
2. User opens the link; `POST /auth/reset-password { token, password }` verifies the token, sets the new password (hashed by the pre-save hook) and invalidates old sessions/refresh tokens.
3. Notify the user by email that the password changed.

### Sending
Use nodemailer or a transactional service (SendGrid, Resend, SES). Never put the token in logs. Rate-limit both endpoints.

Tokens are single-use and expire quickly
Forgot-password responds identically whether the email exists or not
After reset, invalidate old sessions/refresh tokens
Rate-limit email-sending endpoints
pitfalls: Storing the reset token in plain text
Revealing whether an email is registered
Using predictable tokens (Math.random, user id, timestamp)

interview.a: If the database leaks, attackers cannot use the stored hashes to build valid reset links, just like password hashing.

interview.a: To prevent account enumeration: attackers cannot learn which emails are registered by observing different responses.

topics.title: Validation with Zod, Joi and express-validator
topics.summary: Validate and clean req.body, params and query at the edge using a schema library in a reusable middleware.
topics.description:
**Never trust client input.** Every value in `req.body`, `req.params`, `req.query` and headers must be validated for type, shape, range and length before use. Validate at the edge (middleware) so controllers receive clean data.

### Three popular choices
| Library | Style | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Zod** | schema objects, TypeScript-first | `safeParse`, transforms, coercion, inferred types |
| **Joi** | schema objects | mature, rich rules, `abortEarly: false` |
| **express-validator** | chain of checks per field | `body('email').isEmail()`, built on validator.js |

### Why schemas beat manual `if`s
They describe the contract once, return all errors, **strip unknown fields** (stops mass assignment), coerce types (`"5"` -> `5`) and give consistent messages.

### A reusable `validate` middleware
`validate({ body: schema, query: schema, params: schema })` parses each part; on failure respond `400/422` with the list of issues; on success replace the data with the parsed, cleaned values. Remember that in Express 5 `req.query` is a read-only getter, so store parsed query data on another property such as `req.validated.query` (or `res.locals`).

### Validate more than the body
IDs (`ObjectId` format), pagination numbers, enums for sort fields, file mime types and headers.

### Beyond the schema
Validation checks *shape*; business checks (email already used, stock available) still happen in the service layer. Database constraints (unique index) are the final safety net.

Schema libraries return all errors, coerce types and strip unknown keys
Zod = modern/TypeScript, Joi = mature, express-validator = chain style
In Express 5 do not reassign `req.query`; store parsed data elsewhere
Keep database constraints as the last line of defence

Allowing extra fields through (mass assignment)
Trusting numeric strings without coercion/range checks

interview.a: Client checks are only convenience; anyone can call the API directly, so the server must enforce every rule.

interview.q: What does a strict schema protect against?
interview.a: Mass assignment: unknown fields such as role or isAdmin are rejected or stripped instead of reaching the database.

topics.title: Helmet and Rate Limiting
topics.summary: helmet sets safe HTTP security headers; express-rate-limit throttles abuse such as brute-force logins.
topics.description:
### Helmet
**helmet** is a collection of small middleware that set security-related response headers with sensible defaults. One line: `app.use(helmet())`.

| Header | Protects against |
|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | XSS by restricting where scripts/styles can load from |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | forces HTTPS |
| `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | MIME sniffing |
| `X-Frame-Options` / `frame-ancestors` | clickjacking |
| `Referrer-Policy` | leaking URLs to other sites |
| removes `X-Powered-By` | hides the framework |

For a pure JSON API the default CSP is harmless; if you serve a React build from Express you may need to tune CSP directives (images, API origins).

### Rate limiting
A rate limiter counts requests per client (IP or user id) within a time window and answers **429 Too Many Requests** when the limit is exceeded. It reduces brute-force attacks, scraping and accidental overload.

- Apply a general limit to the whole API (for example 100 requests per 15 minutes).
- Apply a **stricter** limit to sensitive routes (`/login`, `/forgot-password`, OTP verification).
- Send standard headers (`RateLimit-*`, `Retry-After`) so clients can back off.
- Behind a proxy set `trust proxy`, otherwise everyone shares the proxy's IP.
- The default store is in memory and per process; with several instances use a shared store such as Redis (`rate-limit-redis`).

### Related defences
Account lockouts, CAPTCHAs, slow-down middleware (`express-slow-down`) and WAF/CDN limits (Cloudflare) at the edge.
keyPoints: `app.use(helmet())` early in the middleware chain
Rate-limit globally and stricter on auth routes
429 + `Retry-After` tells clients to back off
Set `trust proxy` so IPs are real behind proxies
Use a Redis store for multi-instance deployments
pitfalls: Rate limiting by IP without `trust proxy` (all users share one IP)
Per-process memory store in a clustered/Docker-scaled app (limits multiply)
Disabling helmet's CSP because it "breaks things" instead of configuring it

examples.code:
import express from 'express'
import helmet from 'helmet'
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'

const app = express()
app.set('trust proxy', 1)
app.use(helmet())
app.use(express.json())

const apiLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 100,                         // 100 requests / 15 min / IP
  standardHeaders: 'draft-7',
  legacyHeaders: false,
  message: { error: 'Too many requests, please try again later' },
})

const loginLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 5,
  skipSuccessfulRequests: true,       // only failed attempts count
  message: { error: 'Too many login attempts' },
})

app.use('/api', apiLimiter)
app.post('/api/auth/login', loginLimiter, (req, res) => res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid credentials' }))

app.listen(3000)

# HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

# {"error":"Too many login attempts"}

interview.a: It sets protective HTTP headers (CSP, HSTS, nosniff, frame protections and more) to reduce common browser-based attacks.

interview.a: Login endpoints are the main target of brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks, so they need much lower thresholds than normal API routes.

topics.title: CORS: What, Why and How to Configure
topics.summary: Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the server sends CORS headers; configure the cors package with an allow-list.
topics.description:
### The problem
Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: a page at `http://localhost:5173` (React) cannot read responses from `http://localhost:3000` (API), because the *origin* (protocol + host + port) differs. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism by which the **server** opts in by sending headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.

CORS is enforced **by browsers only**. curl, Postman and server-to-server calls ignore it, so it is not an authentication mechanism.

### Simple vs preflighted requests
For "non-simple" requests (methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers like `Authorization`, or `Content-Type: application/json`) the browser first sends an **OPTIONS preflight** asking permission. The server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` and the allowed origin. The `cors` package handles it.

### Using the `cors` package
```js
app.use(cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:5173', credentials: true }))
```
- `origin`: string, array, regex or a function (best for allow-lists).
- `credentials: true`: lets the browser send/receive cookies; then `origin` **cannot** be `*`, and the front end must use `credentials: 'include'` (fetch) or `withCredentials: true` (axios).
- `methods`, `allowedHeaders`, `exposedHeaders`, `maxAge` (cache preflight).

### Rules
- Register `cors()` **before** your routes.
- Use an explicit allow-list from an env variable in production.
- Never combine `origin: '*'` with credentials.
- A "CORS error" for a request that failed with 500 or 404 may simply be a missing header on the error response; check the Network tab.
keyPoints: CORS is a browser rule; the server opts in via response headers
Preflight `OPTIONS` happens for JSON, custom headers and non-simple methods
Cookies need `credentials: true` plus a specific origin (not `*`)
Register `cors()` before routes and use an allow-list in production
It does not protect your API from non-browser clients
pitfalls: `origin: '*'` together with `credentials: true` (browser rejects it)
Forgetting `credentials: 'include'` on the client, so cookies are not sent
Treating CORS as security for the API

interview.a: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests to ask the server whether the actual method and headers are allowed.

interview.a: Browsers reject wildcard origins on credentialed requests; the server must echo one specific allowed origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

topics.title: NoSQL Injection, XSS, CSRF and HPP
topics.summary: Understand and block the classic web attacks: operator injection, script injection, forged requests and parameter pollution.
topics.description:
### NoSQL injection
If you pass JSON straight into a query, a client can send operators instead of values:
`{ "email": "a@x.com", "password": { "$ne": "" } }` makes `User.findOne(req.body)` match without a password. Defences: validate that fields are **strings** (Zod/Joi), cast explicitly (`String(req.body.email)`), whitelist fields, and strip keys starting with `$` or containing `.`. Mongoose `sanitizeFilter: true` neutralises operators in filters. The old `express-mongo-sanitize` package assumed a writable `req.query`, so check compatibility with Express 5 or sanitize yourself.

### XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
Attacker-supplied HTML/JS ends up in a page and runs in other users' browsers, stealing tokens. React escapes output by default; danger comes from `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, server-rendered templates with unescaped output, and stored HTML. Defences: escape output, sanitise rich text (`sanitize-html`, DOMPurify), set a Content Security Policy via helmet, use `httpOnly` cookies.

### CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
A malicious site makes the victim's browser send a request to your API; cookies are attached automatically. It only matters for **cookie-based** auth. Defences: `SameSite=Lax/Strict` cookies, verifying `Origin`/`Referer`, CSRF tokens (double-submit cookie, e.g. `csrf-csrf`; the old `csurf` is deprecated), and requiring a custom header (`X-Requested-With`) that cross-site forms cannot set. Bearer tokens in the `Authorization` header are not affected.

### HPP (HTTP Parameter Pollution)
`?role=user&role=admin` becomes an **array** and can break logic or bypass checks. Validate that expected strings really are strings, or use the `hpp` middleware (check Express 5 support).

### General rule
Treat all input as untrusted, validate strictly, encode on output.

interview.a: Sending query operators (like {"$ne": ""}) where a plain value is expected so the query matches unintended documents; prevent it by validating input types and sanitising filters.

topics.title: Secrets, Environment Variables and OWASP Checklist
topics.summary: Keep secrets out of code, validate config on startup and walk through an OWASP-based security checklist.
topics.description:
### Secrets and environment variables
API keys, database URLs and JWT secrets must **never** be in source control. Store them in environment variables:
- Local: `.env` (ignored by git) loaded with `node --env-file=.env` or `dotenv`.
- Production: the hosting platform's secret manager (Render/Railway/Vercel settings, AWS Secrets Manager, Docker/Kubernetes secrets).
- Commit a `.env.example` listing the variable **names** only.
- Validate required variables at startup with Zod and fail fast; generate secrets with `node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"`.
- If a secret is ever committed, **rotate it** - deleting the file does not remove it from git history.

### OWASP Top 10 checklist (API focus)
| Risk | Express action |
|---|---|
| Broken access control | authZ on every route, ownership checks, deny by default |
| Cryptographic failures | HTTPS only, bcrypt/argon2, strong JWT secrets |
| Injection | validated input, parameterised SQL, `sanitizeFilter` |
| Insecure design | rate limits, least privilege, threat modelling |
| Security misconfiguration | helmet, no stack traces in prod, `NODE_ENV=production` |
| Vulnerable components | `npm audit`, Dependabot, lockfile, update regularly |
| Auth failures | strong passwords, rate-limit login, 2FA, short tokens |
| Integrity failures | verify webhook signatures, pin CI dependencies |
| Logging failures | log auth events, never log secrets/passwords |
| SSRF | never fetch user-supplied URLs without an allow-list |

### Extras
Limit body size, disable `X-Powered-By`, secure cookies, set timeouts, run as non-root in Docker, and keep error messages generic.

Provide `.env.example`; validate env at startup and fail fast
Rotate any leaked secret immediately
Run `npm audit` and keep dependencies updated
Use the OWASP Top 10 as a recurring review checklist
pitfalls: Committing `.env` or hard-coding a fallback secret (`|| 'secret'`) in code
Logging full request bodies or Authorization headers
Leaving `NODE_ENV` unset in production (verbose errors, slower Express)

topics.title: File Uploads with Multer, Safety and Cloud Storage
topics.summary: Accept multipart uploads with multer, enforce size/type limits, and move files to Cloudinary or S3 instead of the server disk.
topics.description:
`express.json()` cannot read files. Uploads use `multipart/form-data`, parsed by **multer**, which adds `req.file` (single) or `req.files` (many) and puts text fields in `req.body`.

### Storage engines
- **diskStorage**: writes to a folder; you control destination and filename.
- **memoryStorage**: keeps a `Buffer` in `req.file.buffer`; good when forwarding straight to cloud storage (keep files small).

### Upload helpers
`upload.single('avatar')`, `upload.array('photos', 5)`, `upload.fields([{ name: 'cover' }, { name: 'docs' }])`. The string must match the form field name.

### File upload safety (important)
1. Set `limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 5 }`.
2. Use `fileFilter` to allow only expected MIME types - but the MIME type comes from the client, so also check the real **magic bytes** (package `file-type`) before trusting an image.
3. **Never** use the original filename for the path: generate a random name (`crypto.randomUUID()`) and keep only a safe extension. Original names can contain `../` or overwrite files.
4. Store uploads **outside** the web root or on object storage; never execute them.
5. Require authentication and rate-limit upload routes.
6. Scan or re-encode images (e.g. with `sharp`) for sensitive apps.

### Cloud storage
Local disks vanish on many hosts (Render, Heroku, containers). Use **Cloudinary** (upload stream, returns a CDN URL and handles image transformations) or **AWS S3 / R2** (store object keys; send the browser a pre-signed URL so large files go straight to storage, bypassing your server).

Save only the resulting URL or key in the database.
keyPoints: multer parses multipart; field name must match `single('name')`
Always set size/count limits and a `fileFilter`
Do not trust the client MIME type or filename; generate your own names
Use memory storage + cloud upload for ephemeral hosts
Store URLs/keys in the DB, not file bytes
pitfalls: Using `file.originalname` as the saved path (path traversal, overwrites)
No size limit (disk exhaustion) or no auth on the upload route
Relying on local disk in containers or serverless where it is wiped
Placing `upload.single()` after the body is already consumed by another parser

interview.a: Both come from the client and can be forged; check magic bytes server-side and generate your own safe filename to prevent disguised files and path traversal.

interview.q: Why use Cloudinary or S3 instead of the server disk?
interview.a: Container and PaaS disks are ephemeral and not shared between instances; object storage is durable, scalable and can serve files via CDN.

topics.title: Real-time: Server-Sent Events and Socket.IO
topics.summary: Push data to browsers with one-way SSE or two-way Socket.IO and attach both to an Express server.
topics.description:
HTTP is request/response, so the server cannot push data by itself. Two common solutions:

### Server-Sent Events (SSE)
A long-lived HTTP response with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`. The server sends text messages; the browser's built-in `EventSource` receives them and **auto-reconnects**. It is **one-way** (server to client) and works over plain HTTP, ideal for notifications, progress bars, live dashboards and AI token streaming.

Message format: `data: <text>\n\n` (a blank line ends one event). Optional `event:` and `id:` fields. Remove the client from your list on `req.on('close')`, and send a periodic comment (`: ping`) to keep proxies from closing the connection. Disable proxy buffering in nginx (`proxy_buffering off`).

### Socket.IO (WebSockets)
A library for **two-way**, low-latency communication with rooms, namespaces, acknowledgements and automatic fallback/reconnection. Use it for chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing.

Setup: wrap the Express app in an `http.Server`, then attach `new Server(httpServer, { cors })`. On `connection` you get a `socket` to `emit` and listen with `on`. `io.to(room).emit()` broadcasts to a room. Authenticate in `io.use((socket, next) => ...)` using a token in `socket.handshake.auth`.

### Which one?
| Need | Choose |
|---|---|
| Server pushes updates only | SSE |
| Client and server both send often | Socket.IO / WebSocket |
| Simple, works with HTTP infra | SSE |
| Rooms, broadcast, presence | Socket.IO |

### Scaling
Several server instances need a shared adapter (Redis adapter for Socket.IO) so broadcasts reach every client.

interview.a: SSE is one-way server-to-client over normal HTTP with built-in reconnection; WebSocket (and Socket.IO) is full duplex, better when the client also sends frequent messages.

interview.q: Why can't you just call app.listen when using Socket.IO?
interview.a: Socket.IO must attach to the underlying HTTP server; create it with http.createServer(app), pass it to Server, and call httpServer.listen.

topics.title: Sending Email with Nodemailer
topics.summary: Send transactional emails (welcome, verify, reset) via SMTP with nodemailer, ideally from a queue.
topics.description:
**Nodemailer** is the standard Node library for sending email over SMTP. In production you connect it to a provider (Gmail app password for demos, SendGrid, Mailgun, Amazon SES, Resend, Brevo) rather than running your own mail server.

### Steps
1. Create a **transporter** once with host, port, and credentials from `.env`.
2. Call `transporter.sendMail({ from, to, subject, text, html })`.
3. Handle failures: email delivery should not make the main request fail unexpectedly.

### Good practices
- Always provide both `text` and `html` versions.
- Use a verified sender domain with SPF/DKIM/DMARC DNS records, otherwise mail lands in spam.
- Escape user-provided values inserted in HTML.
- **Do not make users wait** for SMTP: respond first and send in the background, or push a job to a queue (BullMQ + Redis) with retries.
- Use `jsonTransport` or a fake SMTP (Ethereal, Mailpit, MailHog) in development and tests so no real emails go out.
- Never log full email bodies containing tokens.

### Templates
Generate HTML from template strings, Handlebars/EJS, or the `mjml` library for responsive email layouts.

### Typical emails
Welcome, email verification, password reset, order receipt, notifications. Each should have one clear call to action link.

### Rate limits
Providers cap sending speed; also protect your own endpoints (forgot-password) with rate limiting so attackers cannot use you to spam.
keyPoints: Create one transporter from env credentials
`sendMail` with `text` + `html`; verify the sender domain (SPF/DKIM)
Send in the background or via a queue with retries
Use jsonTransport/Mailpit/Ethereal for dev and tests
Rate-limit endpoints that trigger emails
pitfalls: Awaiting slow SMTP inside the request path for every user action
Committing SMTP passwords
Sending from an unverified domain (spam folder)

interview.q: Why not send emails synchronously inside the request?
interview.a: SMTP calls are slow and can fail; users should not wait or see errors for them, so send in the background or enqueue a retryable job.

interview.q: What are SPF and DKIM?
interview.a: DNS-based mechanisms that prove your mail server is allowed to send for your domain (SPF) and that the message was not altered (DKIM), improving deliverability.

topics.title: Payments: Stripe Checkout and Webhooks
topics.summary: Create a Stripe Checkout session on the server and fulfil orders from a signature-verified webhook that uses the raw body.
topics.description:
Never process card details yourself. **Stripe Checkout** hosts the payment page; your server only creates a session and later learns the result.

### Flow
1. Client calls `POST /api/checkout` (authenticated).
2. Server loads the real prices **from your database** (never trust prices from the client), then calls `stripe.checkout.sessions.create({ mode: 'payment', line_items, success_url, cancel_url, metadata: { orderId } })`.
3. Server returns `session.url`; the browser redirects there.
4. After payment Stripe calls your **webhook** (`checkout.session.completed`).
5. The webhook handler marks the order paid and sends the receipt.

Do not rely on the success redirect to mark orders paid: users can close the tab. The webhook is the source of truth.

### Webhook rules
- Stripe signs each request. Verify with `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, signatureHeader, endpointSecret)`.
- Signature verification needs the **raw body bytes**. So mount `express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })` on the webhook route **before** `express.json()` (or only apply `json()` to other routes). A parsed body will fail verification.
- Respond `2xx` quickly; do heavy work asynchronously. Stripe retries failures.
- Be **idempotent**: the same event can arrive more than once; store processed `event.id`s or make updates safe to repeat.
- Test locally with the Stripe CLI: `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks/stripe`.

### Keys
Use the secret key (`sk_...`) only on the server and the publishable key on the front end; keep `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in env.

interview.q: Why must the webhook use express.raw?
interview.a: Stripe's signature is computed over the exact raw bytes; if express.json() parses the body first, re-serialising it changes the bytes and verification fails.

interview.q: Why use a webhook instead of the redirect to confirm payment?
interview.a: Users may close the browser or lose connection before the redirect, while the webhook is a reliable server-to-server notification that is retried until acknowledged.

topics.title: Scheduled Jobs and Background Tasks (cron)
topics.summary: Run recurring tasks with node-cron, and use queues or a separate worker for heavy or multi-instance workloads.
topics.description:
Some work does not start from an HTTP request: nightly cleanup, daily reports, expiring trials, reminder emails. **node-cron** schedules functions with a cron expression.

### Cron expression
Five fields: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`.
| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `* * * * *` | every minute |
| `*/15 * * * *` | every 15 minutes |
| `0 2 * * *` | daily at 02:00 |
| `0 9 * * 1` | Mondays at 09:00 |
| `0 0 1 * *` | first of every month |

Pass `{ timezone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }`, otherwise the server's time zone is used.

### Rules for jobs
- Wrap the body in `try/catch` and log: an unhandled rejection in a job can crash the process.
- Make jobs **idempotent** (running twice is harmless) and prevent overlap with a lock flag if a run can take longer than the interval.
- Do not schedule jobs in a serverless function: there is no always-on process. Use the platform scheduler (Vercel Cron, GitHub Actions, Render cron job) to hit a protected endpoint or run a script.

### Multiple instances
If you run 3 server instances, a cron inside the app runs **three times**. Options: run jobs in a dedicated worker process, use a distributed lock (Redis `SET NX`), or use a queue such as **BullMQ** (Redis) with repeatable jobs, retries and concurrency control.

### Queues for heavy work
Image processing, PDF generation and bulk email should be pushed to a queue and processed by workers, so the HTTP request returns immediately.

interview.a: Each instance runs the schedule, so the job executes multiple times; use a single worker, a distributed lock or a queue-based scheduler.

interview.q: Why make scheduled jobs idempotent?
interview.a: Jobs may run twice due to retries, restarts or overlap; idempotent logic ensures repeated runs do not corrupt data or duplicate effects.

topics.title: MVC, Folder Structure, Config and Environments
topics.summary: Organise code into routes, controllers, services and models, centralise config, and keep one codebase for dev, test and production.
topics.description:
A single `index.js` works for demos; real APIs need structure so teams can find and change code safely.

### Layers (separation of concerns)
| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Routes** | map URL + method to a controller; attach middleware (auth, validation) |
| **Controllers** | read `req`, call a service, shape the `res` - no business rules |
| **Services** | business logic, orchestration, transactions - no `req`/`res` |
| **Models / repositories** | database access and schemas |
| **Middleware** | cross-cutting concerns (auth, errors, logging) |
| **Utils / config** | helpers, env loading, constants |

This is **MVC** adapted for APIs: the "view" is simply the JSON response.

### Recommended folder layout
Two common styles: **by type** (`controllers/`, `models/`, `routes/`) for small apps, and **by feature** (`modules/users/{user.routes.js, user.controller.js, user.service.js, user.model.js}`) for larger ones - everything about a feature lives together.

### Config module
Read `process.env` in **one** file, validate it, export a frozen object, and import `config` everywhere else. Do not scatter `process.env.X` through the code.

### Environments
Use `NODE_ENV` (`development`, `test`, `production`) and separate env files or platform variables per stage: different database URIs, secrets, log levels and CORS origins. Always set `NODE_ENV=production` in production: Express then caches views and error handling is leaner.

### Dependency direction
Routes -> controllers -> services -> models. Lower layers never import upper layers.

topics.title: Logging with morgan and pino, Health and Monitoring
topics.summary: Log HTTP requests and application events as structured JSON, correlate them with request ids and expose health checks.
topics.description:
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Production needs useful, safe logs and basic monitoring.

### HTTP request logs: morgan
`morgan('dev')` prints a coloured line per request in development; `morgan('combined')` writes Apache-style access logs. It is a middleware that logs method, URL, status and response time.

### Structured application logs: pino
`console.log` is unstructured and slow. **pino** is a very fast JSON logger with levels (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `fatal`). JSON lines can be searched and aggregated by Datadog, Loki, CloudWatch or ELK. **pino-http** logs every request as JSON and attaches `req.log`, a child logger that includes the request id. In development use `pino-pretty` for readable output.

### What to log
- Requests (method, path, status, duration), errors with stack traces, auth events (login failures), slow queries, job runs.
- **Never log**: passwords, tokens, full card data, whole request bodies. Use pino's `redact` option for paths such as `req.headers.authorization`.

### Request id
Generate or accept `X-Request-Id`, attach it to every log line and return it in the response, so a user report can be traced across services.

### Health checks
`GET /health` (liveness: process is up) and `GET /ready` (readiness: DB reachable). Load balancers and Kubernetes use them to route traffic and restart pods.

### Monitoring
Track error rate, latency percentiles, memory and CPU. Tools: Sentry (exceptions), Prometheus + Grafana (`prom-client` metrics), Datadog/New Relic (APM), uptime monitors (UptimeRobot, Better Stack).

interview.a: JSON logs are machine-searchable and aggregatable (by level, request id, user), unlike free-text console output.

interview.q: Liveness vs readiness probes?
interview.a: Liveness tells the orchestrator the process is alive (restart if not); readiness says it can serve traffic (dependencies like the DB are reachable), so load balancers route only to ready instances.

topics.title: API Docs with Swagger / OpenAPI
topics.summary: Describe endpoints with OpenAPI and serve an interactive Swagger UI so frontend developers can explore and test the API.
topics.description:
**OpenAPI** (formerly Swagger) is a standard, language-neutral format (YAML/JSON) describing an API: paths, parameters, request/response schemas, auth. **Swagger UI** renders it as an interactive page where you can click "Try it out".

### Why
- Frontend and mobile developers get an always-current contract.
- Clients and tests can be generated from the spec.
- It doubles as living documentation and design review material.

### Two ways to produce the spec
1. **Code-first**: write JSDoc comments (`@openapi` blocks) above routes and let **swagger-jsdoc** collect them.
2. **Spec-first**: maintain `openapi.yaml` manually (or generate from Zod schemas with libraries such as `zod-to-openapi`) and load it.

### Serving it
`swagger-ui-express` mounts the UI: `app.use('/api-docs', swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(spec))`. Often exposed only in development/staging, or behind authentication in production.

### Describe
- `servers` (base URL), `components.securitySchemes` (Bearer JWT), `components.schemas` (reusable models like `User`, `Error`), each operation's `summary`, `tags`, `parameters`, `requestBody`, `responses` (200, 400, 401, 404).
- Add `security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }]` to protected routes so the "Authorize" button works.

### Tip
Keep docs close to the route code (or generated from the same schemas) so they do not drift.

interview.q: What is the difference between Swagger and OpenAPI?
interview.a: OpenAPI is the specification for describing REST APIs; Swagger is the tool family (Swagger UI, Editor, Codegen) that originally defined and now implements it.

interview.q: Code-first vs spec-first documentation?
interview.a: Code-first generates the spec from annotations or schemas in code (less drift); spec-first designs the OpenAPI document before coding and treats it as the contract.

topics.title: Response Envelope, Pagination and Versioning Standards
topics.summary: Agree on one JSON shape for success and errors, one pagination format and a versioning policy so clients stay simple.
topics.description:
Consistency is what makes an API pleasant. Decide the rules once and apply them everywhere.

### Response envelope
Wrap responses in a predictable shape:
```json
{ "status": "success", "data": { ... }, "meta": { "page": 1 } }
{ "status": "error",   "message": "Validation failed", "errors": [ ... ] }
```
Pros: clients can add metadata (pagination, request id) without breaking changes, and handle errors uniformly. Some teams prefer returning the bare resource and using HTTP status codes plus a standard error body (RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`). Pick one and be consistent.

### Helpers
Small functions `ok(res, data, meta)`, `created(res, data)` and the central error handler keep controllers tidy and the shape identical.

### Pagination standard
- Request: `?page=2&limit=20` (offset) or `?cursor=abc&limit=20` (cursor).
- Response `meta`: `page`, `limit`, `total`, `totalPages`, plus `hasNext`. Or `Link` headers (`rel="next"`) and `X-Total-Count`.
- Enforce a **maximum limit** and a sensible default.

### Naming and formats
Plural nouns, `camelCase` JSON keys, ISO-8601 dates in UTC, ids as strings, money in the smallest unit (cents/paise), `null` for missing values.

### Versioning policy
Prefix with `/api/v1`. Additive changes (new fields, new endpoints) are non-breaking; removing or renaming fields, or changing semantics, requires `/api/v2`. Announce deprecations with a `Deprecation`/`Sunset` header and keep the old version running for a defined period.

Returning HTTP 200 with `status: "error"` in the body
Changing field meaning in-place without a version bump

interview.a: A fixed wrapper (status, data, meta) around every response; it lets you add metadata like pagination without breaking clients and keeps error handling uniform.

topics.title: Testing with Vitest/Jest and supertest
topics.summary: Test routes without opening a port using supertest, cover happy and error paths, and isolate the database.
topics.description:
Automated tests protect an API from regressions. For Express the usual stack is a test runner (**Vitest** or **Jest**) plus **supertest**, which sends HTTP requests directly to your `app` object - no `listen()` needed. This is why you export `app` separately from `server.js`.

### Kinds of tests
| Level | What | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | one function (service, util) with mocks | Vitest/Jest |
| Integration | route + middleware + DB together | supertest + test DB |
| End-to-end | deployed app, real client | Playwright/Cypress/Postman |

### Writing an integration test
1. Import `app`.
2. `await request(app).post('/api/tasks').send({...})`.
3. Assert on status, headers and body.

Test the unhappy paths as much as the happy ones: validation errors (400), missing auth (401), forbidden (403), not found (404), duplicates (409).

### Database in tests
Never touch the development database. Options: **mongodb-memory-server** (in-memory MongoDB), a dedicated test database that is cleaned before each test, or Testcontainers/Docker. Use `NODE_ENV=test` to load test configuration, and reset data in `beforeEach`.

### Mocking
Mock external services (email, Stripe, S3) with `vi.mock` / `jest.mock` so tests are fast and deterministic.

### Auth in tests
Create a user and sign a token in a helper, then call `.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + token)`.

### CI
Run `npm test` on every pull request; track coverage but do not chase 100 percent.

topics.title: Dockerizing an Express App
topics.summary: Package the API into a small, secure image and run it with MongoDB using docker compose.
topics.description:
**Docker** packages your app with its exact Node version and dependencies into an **image** that runs the same on your laptop, CI and the cloud.

### A good Dockerfile
1. Start from a slim base: `node:24-alpine` (or `-slim`).
2. Copy `package*.json` first and run `npm ci --omit=dev` - Docker caches this layer, so rebuilds are fast unless dependencies change.
3. Copy the source after installing.
4. Set `NODE_ENV=production`, `EXPOSE` the port, and run as the non-root `node` user.
5. Start with `CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]` (exec form) so signals like SIGTERM reach Node and graceful shutdown works. Avoid `npm start` as PID 1.

### `.dockerignore`
Exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, logs and tests so the build context is small and secrets are never copied into the image.

### Multi-stage builds
Use one stage to build (TypeScript, dev dependencies) and a final lean stage that copies only the output and production dependencies.

### docker compose
Define the API and its dependencies (MongoDB, Redis) in `compose.yaml`. Services reach each other by service name (`mongodb://mongo:27017/app`). Use a named volume so database data survives container recreation. Pass configuration via `environment:` or `env_file`, never bake secrets into the image.

### Health check
Add a `HEALTHCHECK` (or compose `healthcheck`) hitting `/health`.

### Bind to all interfaces
Inside a container, listen on `0.0.0.0` (the default for `app.listen(port)`), and map the port with `-p 3000:3000`.

topics.title: PM2, nginx Reverse Proxy and CI/CD
topics.summary: Run Node under PM2 (cluster mode), put nginx in front for HTTPS and static files, and automate deploys with GitHub Actions.
topics.description:
### PM2: process manager
Node runs on one CPU core and dies on crashes. **PM2** keeps it alive and uses all cores:
- `pm2 start src/server.js -i max` starts one worker per core (cluster mode) sharing the same port.
- Auto-restart on crash, restart on memory limit (`--max-memory-restart 300M`), log management, `pm2 reload` for zero-downtime restarts, `pm2 startup` + `pm2 save` to survive reboots.
- Configure via `ecosystem.config.cjs`.

Cluster mode means in-memory state (sessions, rate-limit counters, caches) is **per worker**, so use Redis or the database for shared state. Containers/Kubernetes often replace PM2: run one process per container and scale containers.

### nginx: reverse proxy
Public traffic hits **nginx** on ports 80/443, which forwards to Node on `localhost:3000`:
- **TLS termination** with Let's Encrypt certificates (certbot).
- Serves the React build and static assets quickly, with gzip/brotli and caching.
- Passes `X-Forwarded-For` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers: set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` in Express.
- Request size limits, rate limiting, WebSocket upgrade headers for Socket.IO.

### CI/CD
**CI** (continuous integration) runs lint and tests on each push; **CD** (continuous delivery) deploys when `main` passes. A GitHub Actions workflow typically: checkout, set up Node with cache, `npm ci`, `npm test`, build/push a Docker image, then SSH to the server (or call the platform's deploy hook) and `pm2 reload`.

Store credentials in GitHub **Secrets**, never in the repository.

topics.title: Redis Caching and Performance Tuning
topics.summary: Cache expensive reads in Redis (cache-aside), and apply the main Express performance rules.
topics.description:
### Redis cache-aside
**Redis** is an in-memory key-value store. The most common pattern is **cache-aside**:
1. Build a key (`products:list:page=1`).
2. Try `redis.get(key)`. On a hit, return it immediately.
3. On a miss, query the database, `redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(data), 'EX', 60)`, return.
4. When data changes, **invalidate** (`del`) the affected keys.

Always set a TTL, so stale data eventually disappears. Cache what is read often and changes rarely (product lists, config, expensive aggregations). Do not cache per-user private data under shared keys. Redis is also used for sessions, rate limiting, queues (BullMQ), pub/sub and distributed locks. If Redis is down, the app should fall back to the database, not crash.

### Express performance checklist
- `NODE_ENV=production`.
- Use `compression` (or let nginx do it).
- Never block the event loop: avoid sync functions (`fs.readFileSync`, `bcrypt.hashSync`, big JSON loops) on request paths; move CPU work to worker threads or queues.
- Index database fields used in filters/sorts; paginate; use `.lean()` and field selection; avoid N+1 queries (use `populate`/`$lookup`/`include`).
- Reuse connections (one pool/client).
- HTTP caching: ETag, `Cache-Control`, CDN for static files and public GETs.
- Run multiple processes (PM2 cluster / containers) and scale horizontally.
- Keep payloads small; stream large responses.
- Measure first: `clinic.js`, `autocannon`, APM traces and slow-query logs.
keyPoints: Cache-aside: get -> miss -> DB -> set with TTL -> invalidate on writes
Always use TTLs; handle Redis failures gracefully
Never block the event loop with sync or CPU-heavy code
Index, paginate and avoid N+1 queries
Measure with autocannon/clinic before optimising
pitfalls: Caching without invalidation (users see stale data forever)
Shared cache keys for user-specific responses
Premature optimisation without profiling

interview.a: The application checks the cache first; on a miss it loads from the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns it; writes invalidate or update the cached entries.

interview.q: Name common causes of slow Express APIs.
interview.a: Blocking the event loop with sync/CPU work, missing database indexes, N+1 queries, large uncompressed payloads, and creating connections per request.

topics.title: React to Express: CORS, Vite Proxy, fetch and axios
topics.summary: Call your Express API from a Vite React app either through a dev proxy or CORS, using fetch or an axios instance.
topics.description:
In development you run two servers: Express on `http://localhost:3000` and Vite on `http://localhost:5173`. Different ports mean different **origins**, so the browser applies CORS rules. There are two clean solutions.

### Option A: Vite dev proxy (recommended in development)
Vite forwards `/api/*` calls to Express, so the browser thinks everything is same-origin: no CORS, and cookies just work.

```js
// vite.config.js
server: { proxy: { '/api': { target: 'http://localhost:3000', changeOrigin: true } } }
```
React then calls `fetch('/api/products')`. In production the same relative URL works if Express serves the build or nginx routes `/api` to Node.

### Option B: CORS
Allow the Vite origin in Express (`cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:5173', credentials: true })`) and call the absolute URL from React. Needed when the front end and API live on different domains in production (for example Vercel + Render).

### fetch
Built in; does not reject on 4xx/5xx - check `res.ok` yourself. Send JSON with the header `Content-Type: application/json` and `JSON.stringify`. Add `credentials: 'include'` when using cookies across origins.

### axios
Create one **instance** with `baseURL` and `withCredentials: true`; axios rejects on non-2xx, parses JSON automatically and supports interceptors (attach tokens, handle 401 globally).

### Data fetching in React
Fetch inside `useEffect` (with `AbortController` cleanup) or use **TanStack Query** for caching, retries and loading/error states.

### Error shape
Because the API returns a consistent `{ message }` error, the front end can show `err.response.data.message` anywhere.

Cross-domain production: configure `cors` with `credentials: true`

topics.title: Auth Flow End to End (Cookies + JWT)
topics.summary: Keep the access token in memory and the refresh token in an httpOnly cookie, with an axios interceptor that refreshes on 401.
topics.description:
A secure and popular SPA pattern:

| Token | Where it lives | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Access token (15 min) | React **memory** (state / module variable) | not readable from storage by XSS; sent as `Authorization: Bearer` |
| Refresh token (7 days) | **httpOnly, secure, sameSite cookie** scoped to `/api/auth` | JavaScript cannot read it; browser sends it only to the refresh endpoint |

### The flow
1. **Login**: `POST /api/auth/login` -> server sets the refresh cookie, returns `{ accessToken, user }`. React stores the token in memory.
2. **API calls**: an axios request interceptor adds `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
3. **Expiry**: the API answers `401`. A response interceptor calls `POST /api/auth/refresh` (cookie sent automatically), saves the new token and **retries** the original request once. Several parallel 401s should share one refresh call.
4. **Page reload**: memory is lost, so on startup the app calls `/auth/refresh` to restore the session (show a loading screen meanwhile).
5. **Logout**: `POST /api/auth/logout` clears the cookie server-side; React clears memory.

### Protecting routes
An `AuthContext` exposes `user`, `login`, `logout`, `loading`. A `ProtectedRoute` component redirects to `/login` when there is no user (and waits while `loading`). Remember this is only UX: the **server** must enforce access.

### Cross-site cookies
If front end and API are on different sites in production, the cookie needs `sameSite: 'none'` + `secure: true`, `cors({ credentials: true, origin })`, and `withCredentials: true` in axios. Using the same parent domain (`app.example.com` + `api.example.com`) or serving both from one origin avoids most problems.

Interceptor: attach Bearer token; on 401 refresh once and retry
Restore the session on page load via the refresh endpoint
AuthContext + ProtectedRoute for UX; server enforces real security

pitfalls: Storing tokens in `localStorage` (readable by any XSS)
Infinite refresh loops when the refresh endpoint itself returns 401
Race conditions: several requests refreshing at once
Forgetting `withCredentials`, so the refresh cookie is never sent

interview.q: Why not store the JWT in localStorage?
interview.a: Any XSS vulnerability can read localStorage and steal the token; keeping the access token in memory and the refresh token in an httpOnly cookie greatly reduces that risk.

interview.q: How does the app stay logged in after a page refresh?
interview.a: On startup it calls the refresh endpoint; the browser sends the httpOnly cookie, and if it is valid the server returns a new access token and user data.

topics.title: Serving the React Build from Express and Deploying MERN
topics.summary: Serve Vite's dist folder from Express with an SPA fallback, or deploy front end and API separately.
topics.description:
### Option 1: one server (Express serves React)
Run `npm run build` in the React app, which creates `dist/` (static HTML, JS and CSS). Express serves it:
1. `express.static(distPath)` for assets.
2. API routes under `/api` **before** the fallback.
3. A catch-all `GET` that returns `index.html`, so client-side routes like `/dashboard` work on refresh (**SPA fallback**).

Advantages: same origin (no CORS, simple cookies), one deployment. Disadvantages: front end and API scale and deploy together.

In Express 5 the catch-all syntax is `/{*splat}` (the v4 `'*'` throws). Also return a JSON 404 for unknown `/api/*` routes instead of the HTML page.

### Option 2: separate deployments
- Front end: Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages (static hosting + CDN). Add a rewrite rule `/* -> /index.html` for SPA routing.
- API: Render, Railway, Fly.io, a VPS or AWS. Database: MongoDB Atlas.
- Configure CORS with the front end origin, cookies with `sameSite: 'none'; secure`, and set `VITE_API_URL` to the API URL at **build time**.

### Deployment checklist
1. `NODE_ENV=production`, strong secrets, `trust proxy` set.
2. Atlas network access allows the host; use a dedicated database user.
3. Build command (`npm run build`) and start command (`node src/server.js`) set on the host.
4. HTTPS enabled; health check endpoint configured.
5. Remember free tiers sleep: first request can be slow.

topics.title: Environment Variables on Both Sides
topics.summary: Understand which variables are secret server runtime values and which are public build-time values in Vite.
topics.description:
A MERN project has **two** environments with very different rules.

### Backend (Node/Express)
Variables live on the server and are read at **runtime** from `process.env`: `MONGO_URI`, `JWT_ACCESS_SECRET`, `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `CLIENT_URL`. They are secret and never reach the browser. Load from `.env` in development (`node --env-file=.env` or dotenv) and from the host's settings in production.

### Frontend (Vite/React)
Vite reads `.env` files at **build time** and only exposes variables that start with `VITE_`, through `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` (not `process.env`). Everything you expose is **public**: it is baked into the JavaScript bundle and visible to every visitor. Therefore:
- Never put secrets in `VITE_` variables (no database URLs, JWT secrets, Stripe *secret* keys).
- Public values are fine: API base URL, Stripe *publishable* key, Google client id, feature flags.
- Changing a value requires **rebuilding** the front end.

### Files
`.env` (shared defaults), `.env.development`, `.env.production`, plus `.env.local` for personal overrides (git-ignored). `import.meta.env.MODE`, `DEV` and `PROD` tell you the mode.

### Keeping both sides in sync
- `CLIENT_URL` (server) must equal the front end origin for CORS.
- `VITE_API_URL` (client) must point to the API (or be empty when using a proxy/same origin).
- Provide `.env.example` in both folders; add real `.env` files to `.gitignore`.

### Deployment
Set server variables in the API host's dashboard and `VITE_*` variables in the front end host's **build** settings.

Client: `import.meta.env.VITE_X`, public, build-time

topics.title: Project 1: Todo REST API
topics.summary: A complete Todo API with MongoDB: CRUD, filters, search, pagination, validation and a central error handler.
topics.description:
This first project puts routing, middleware, Mongoose and error handling together in a small but properly structured API. It is the best template for your first real backend.

### Features
- `POST /api/todos` create, `GET /api/todos` list, `GET /api/todos/:id` read one
- `PATCH /api/todos/:id` update, `PATCH /api/todos/:id/toggle` flip completed, `DELETE /api/todos/:id` remove
- List supports `?completed=true`, `?priority=high`, `?search=milk`, `?sort=-createdAt`, `?page=1&limit=10`
- Validation through the Mongoose schema; whitelist of updatable fields
- Consistent JSON errors: 400 invalid data/id, 404 missing todo

### Design choices
1. **App and server are separate** (`app.js` exports the app) so you can add tests later.
2. **Express 5 async controllers**: plain `async` functions; any rejected promise reaches the error handler, so there is no try/catch boilerplate.
3. **Field whitelist** (`pick`) prevents clients from writing fields such as `_id` or `createdAt`.

topics.title: Project 2: Blog API with Authentication
topics.summary: Users register and log in with JWT, write posts with slugs and tags, comment, and only owners or admins can modify content.
topics.description:
The Blog API adds the pieces most real backends need: **authentication, authorization, relations and public/private routes**.

### Features
- Auth: `POST /api/auth/register`, `POST /api/auth/login`, `GET /api/auth/me` (JWT bearer token, bcrypt hashing)
- Posts: public list (published only) with `?tag=`, `?search=`, pagination; read by **slug**; create/update/delete for logged-in users
- **Ownership rules**: only the author or an admin can edit or delete a post
- Comments: `GET/POST /api/posts/:slug/comments`, `DELETE /api/comments/:id` (author of the comment or admin)
- Author data is attached with `populate`, never the password hash

### Design choices
1. **Slugs**: readable URLs (`my-first-post-a1b2c3`) built from the title plus a short random suffix to stay unique.
2. **`protect` middleware** verifies the token and loads the user; **`restrictTo`** is a factory for role checks.
3. **Separate Comment collection** (references post + author) because comments grow without bound; this avoids huge documents.
4. **Registration cannot set `role`**; promote an admin manually in the database or with a seed script.
5. Same error shape everywhere: `{ message }`, with a small `AppError` helper.

### Extend it
Refresh tokens, likes, image upload with multer, draft/published workflow, full-text search with a text index, rate limiting on `/auth/login`.

pitfalls: Returning the password hash (keep `select: false`)
Using the Mongo `_id` for public post URLs and leaking enumeration
Forgetting the ownership check, letting any user delete any post

topics.title: Project 3: E-commerce API (Products, Cart, Orders)
topics.summary: An online-store backend: admin-managed products, a per-user cart, stock-safe checkout and order history.
topics.description:
This project models the core of a shop and shows how to protect **data integrity** when money and stock are involved.

### Features
- Auth with JWT (`customer` and `admin` roles)
- Products: public list with `category`, price range, search, sort and pagination; admin create/update/delete
- Cart (per logged-in user): `GET /api/cart`, `POST /api/cart/items`, `PATCH /api/cart/items/:productId`, `DELETE /api/cart/items/:productId`
- Orders: `POST /api/orders` converts the cart to an order; `GET /api/orders` shows the user's history; admin can mark orders shipped

### Key design decisions
1. **Price snapshot**: each order item stores the product name and price **at purchase time**, so later price changes do not rewrite history.
2. **Server-side totals**: the client sends no prices; the server reads them from the database.
3. **Atomic stock decrement**: `updateOne({ _id, stock: { $gte: qty } }, { $inc: { stock: -qty } })` succeeds only if enough stock remains, preventing overselling under concurrency. If any line fails, previously reserved lines are restored (a compensation step). On a replica set you can wrap this in a MongoDB transaction instead.
4. **Money in the smallest unit** (paise/cents, integers) to avoid floating point errors.
5. **One cart per user** with a unique index on `user`.
6. Orders have a status lifecycle: `pending` -> `shipped` (extend with `paid`, `cancelled`).

### Extend it
Stripe Checkout and webhook, address and shipping, coupons, product images with multer + Cloudinary, order emails with nodemailer.

Atomic conditional `$inc` prevents overselling; compensate on failure
Order status lifecycle and history endpoint
pitfalls: Trusting prices or totals sent by the browser
Check-then-update stock in two steps (race condition)
Storing money as floating-point numbers

topics.title: Project 4: URL Shortener
topics.summary: Shorten links with random codes, redirect with click tracking, optional expiry via a TTL index and a secret token to delete.
topics.description:
A URL shortener is a classic interview project because it is small but touches many backend ideas: unique ids, redirects, atomic counters, validation and abuse control.

### Features
- `POST /api/links` with `{ url, customCode?, expiresInDays? }` returns the short URL and a private `manageToken`
- `GET /:code` redirects (HTTP 302) and counts the click
- `GET /api/links/:code/stats` shows clicks, creation time and last click
- `DELETE /api/links/:code` needs the `x-manage-token` header received at creation time (no user accounts needed)
- Rate limit on link creation

### Design choices
1. **Random base62 codes** of 7 characters (about 3.5 trillion combinations) built with `crypto.randomInt`; a duplicate-key error triggers a retry.
2. **302, not 301**: a permanent redirect would be cached by browsers and clicks would no longer reach your server.
3. **Atomic counter**: `findOneAndUpdate` with `$inc` increments and reads in a single database operation, so parallel clicks are never lost.
4. **Validation**: only `http:` and `https:` URLs, max length 2048, reserved words blocked from custom codes. Reject non-web schemes such as `javascript:`.
5. **Expiry**: a MongoDB **TTL index** on `expiresAt` deletes documents automatically; the handler also answers `410 Gone` during the short window before deletion.
6. **Manage token** is stored only as a SHA-256 hash and compared in constant time.
7. The `/:code` route is registered last so it never shadows `/api` or `/health`.

### Extend it
User accounts, link analytics by day (aggregation), QR codes, Redis caching of hot codes, a React front end.
keyPoints: Random base62 codes with retry on duplicate key
302 redirect + atomic `$inc` click counter
Allow only http/https URLs; block reserved custom codes
TTL index for automatic expiry; 410 for expired links
Hash the manage token; constant-time comparison
pitfalls: Using 301 and losing click statistics to browser caching
Sequential ids that are guessable and enumerable
Accepting any URL scheme (javascript:, file:) or unlimited creation without rate limiting

topics.title: Project 5: Notes App with JWT and Zod Validation
topics.summary: A multi-user notes API: JWT auth, Zod-validated input, per-user data isolation, tags, pinning, archive, search and pagination.
topics.description:
The Notes API focuses on **multi-tenant data safety**: every user sees only their own notes, input is validated with a schema library, and brute-force protection guards the login.

### Features
- `POST /api/auth/register`, `POST /api/auth/login`, `GET /api/auth/me` using bcrypt and a JWT bearer token
- Notes CRUD: `GET/POST /api/notes`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/notes/:id`
- Filters: `?q=` text search, `?tag=`, `?pinned=true`, `?archived=true`, plus pagination
- Pinned notes sort first, then most recently updated
- Login rate limit (10 failed attempts per 15 minutes)

### Design choices
1. **Owner filter everywhere**: every query includes `owner: req.user.id`. A note belonging to someone else behaves exactly like a missing note (404), so ids cannot be probed.
2. **Zod schemas + `validate` middleware**: bodies are checked, trimmed, typed and stripped of unknown keys before reaching controllers (this blocks mass assignment and NoSQL operator injection because values must be strings).
3. **Express 5 detail**: `req.query` is read-only, so the validated query is stored in `req.validated.query` rather than overwriting `req.query`.
4. **Partial updates** use a separate schema built from the same fields **without defaults** and made `.partial()`. (Zod keeps `.default()` values after `.partial()`, so reusing the create schema would silently reset omitted fields to their defaults on every PATCH.)
5. **Generic login errors** and constant response for wrong email vs wrong password.

### Extend it
Refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, note sharing, markdown rendering, soft delete with a trash view, and a React front end using the auth flow from the MERN section.
keyPoints: JWT bearer auth with bcrypt-hashed passwords
Every query filtered by `owner`: users never see others' notes
Zod schemas validate and strip input; `.partial()` for PATCH
Validated query stored on `req.validated` (Express 5 getter)
Login rate limiting with `skipSuccessfulRequests`
pitfalls: Looking up notes by `_id` only (any user could read any note)
Returning 403 for other users' notes (confirms the id exists); prefer 404
Passing `req.query` straight into `find()`
Deriving the PATCH schema with `.partial()` from a schema that has `.default()`s (omitted fields get overwritten)

topics.title: Project 6: Real-time Chat App (Socket.IO + MongoDB)
topics.summary: Rooms, JWT-authenticated sockets, persisted messages with history API, presence and typing indicators, plus a tiny browser client.
topics.description:
This project combines Express (REST) and Socket.IO (real-time) in a single server and persists chat history in MongoDB.

### Features
- REST: `POST /api/auth/register`, `POST /api/auth/login`, `GET /api/rooms/:room/messages?before=<id>&limit=30` (history, newest page first)
- Socket events: `room:join`, `room:leave`, `message:send`, `typing`
- Server events: `message:new`, `room:users` (presence list), `typing`, `system`
- Sockets authenticate with the same JWT as the REST API
- Static browser client in `public/` served by Express

### Design choices
1. **One HTTP server** hosts both Express and Socket.IO: `http.createServer(app)` then `new Server(httpServer)`.
2. **Handshake auth**: a Socket.IO middleware verifies `socket.handshake.auth.token`, loads the user and stores it in `socket.data.user`. Unauthenticated sockets never connect.
3. **Server-side checks** on every event: the sender must actually be in the room, the room name must match a safe pattern, and text is trimmed and limited to 500 characters. Never trust identity or room data sent by the client; the user comes from `socket.data`.
4. **Acknowledgements**: `socket.emit(event, data, callback)` lets the client know whether a message was accepted.
5. **Persistence and history**: messages are saved before being broadcast; cursor pagination (`before=<id>`) loads older messages efficiently.
6. **Presence** is derived from the adapter's room membership and broadcast after join/leave/disconnect.
7. Escape on output: the client uses `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, to avoid XSS from chat text.

### Scaling note
With several server instances use the Socket.IO Redis adapter so broadcasts reach all clients.
keyPoints: Express + Socket.IO share one `http.Server`
Authenticate sockets in `io.use` with the JWT from `handshake.auth`
Use `socket.data.user` (not client-supplied names) and verify room membership
Persist messages, serve history with cursor pagination
Render chat text with `textContent` to prevent XSS
pitfalls: Trusting a `username` field sent in the message payload
Broadcasting before validating or saving the message
Using `innerHTML` for incoming messages on the client

topics.description:
A reusable microservice that other apps call to store images and PDFs. It brings together every file-upload safety rule.

### Features
- `POST /api/files` multipart upload (field `files`, up to 5 per request, 5 MB each)
- `GET /api/files` list your files with pagination, `GET /api/files/:id` metadata
- `GET /api/files/:id/content` inline view, `GET /api/files/:id/download` forced download
- `DELETE /api/files/:id` removes the record and the file
- Authentication with an `x-api-key` header (keys come from `API_KEYS` in `.env`)
- Storage quota of 20 MB per owner

### Design choices
1. **Never trust the client**: multer limits size and count, but the real type is detected by reading the first bytes (**magic numbers**) of the saved file: PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and PDF are accepted, everything else is deleted immediately.
2. **Random storage names**: files are saved as UUIDs without extensions inside `uploads/`; the original name is kept only as metadata (sanitised) and used in the download header. This blocks path traversal and overwrites.
3. **Served with the detected MIME type**, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and anything that is not an image is forced to download rather than rendered inline.
4. **Ownership**: the owner id is derived from the API key hash; every query includes it, and a file of another owner is a 404.
5. **Quota** is calculated with an aggregation (`$sum` of sizes) before accepting new files.
6. **Partial success**: a request with one bad file still stores the good ones and reports `rejected` entries.
7. Multer errors (`LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`, `LIMIT_FILE_COUNT`) are translated into proper 4xx responses.

### Production notes
Swap local disk for S3/Cloudinary (store the object key), add virus scanning, and send files through a CDN.
keyPoints: multer limits + magic-byte detection after upload
Random UUID storage names; original name only as metadata
Serve detected MIME, nosniff, force download for non-images
Owner-scoped queries; quota via aggregation
Translate MulterError codes into 4xx responses
pitfalls: Trusting `file.mimetype` or the extension from the client
Saving with `originalname` (traversal, overwrites, double extensions)
Serving user HTML/SVG inline from your own origin (stored XSS)

topics.title: Project 8: Complete MERN Auth Boilerplate
topics.summary: Production-style authentication starter: email verification, access + rotating refresh tokens, password reset, roles, security middleware and a React client.
topics.description:
This capstone is a reusable starter for any MERN product. The server is Express 5 + MongoDB; the client is Vite + React with protected routes.

### What it includes
- **Register** with email verification (token emailed; in development the link is printed in the server log)
- **Login** that is blocked until the email is verified; generic error messages
- **Short-lived access JWT** (15 min) sent as `Authorization: Bearer`
- **Opaque refresh token** in an `httpOnly` cookie scoped to `/api/auth`; stored **hashed** in MongoDB, **rotated** on every refresh and deleted on logout
- **Forgot / reset password** (hashed single-use token, all sessions revoked after reset)
- Roles (`user`, `admin`), `protect` and `restrictTo` middleware, `GET /api/users/me`, `PATCH /api/users/me`, admin-only `GET /api/admin/users`
- Security: helmet, CORS allow-list with credentials, rate limiting, Zod validation with strict schemas, validated environment variables, bcrypt cost 12

### Design choices
1. **Opaque refresh tokens** (random bytes) instead of JWTs: they can be revoked individually by deleting a database row, and a database leak exposes only hashes.
2. **Atomic rotation**: `findOneAndDelete` on the token hash means a stolen token cannot be refreshed twice in parallel.
3. **Tokens in emails** are random, hashed in the database and expire.
4. **The client** keeps the access token in memory only, restores the session through the refresh endpoint on page load, and retries failed requests once after refreshing (see the MERN section).
5. **Environment validation** makes the server fail fast if a secret is missing or too short.

### Next steps
Social login with Passport, 2FA (TOTP), account lockout, audit log of sessions, email templates, and tests with supertest.
keyPoints: Access JWT in memory; refresh token in httpOnly cookie, hashed in DB, rotated each use
Email verification and password reset with hashed, expiring, single-use tokens
Zod strict schemas, helmet, CORS credentials allow-list, rate limits
Fail-fast env validation with Zod
React: AuthContext, axios interceptor with single-flight refresh, ProtectedRoute
pitfalls: Setting `sameSite: 'none'` without `secure: true` for cross-site deployments
Forgetting `withCredentials: true` on the client, so the refresh cookie is never sent
Revealing whether an email exists in forgot-password responses
Leaving verification links only in logs in production (wire up real email)

interview.a: They can be revoked individually (delete the row), rotated on every use, and a database leak exposes only hashes; a long-lived JWT cannot be revoked before it expires.

topics.title: Express Interview Questions: Rapid-Fire Round
topics.summary: A compact set of the most common Express and Node backend interview questions with crisp answers and a coding exercise.
topics.description:
Use this page as a last-minute revision sheet. Say the short answer first, then add one detail or example.

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What is middleware? | A function `(req, res, next)` in the request pipeline; it can change req/res, end the request or call `next()`. |
| Order of middleware? | Registration order; parsers and security first, routes, 404, error handler last. |
| `app.use` vs `app.get`? | `use` matches every method and any path prefix; `get` matches only GET on the exact route. |
| `req.params` vs `req.query` vs `req.body`? | Path segments, the part after `?`, and the parsed payload. |
| How do you handle errors? | Throw or `next(err)`; one 4-argument error handler at the end; Express 5 forwards rejected promises. |
| 401 vs 403? | Not authenticated vs authenticated but not allowed. |
| What is CORS? | A browser rule; the server sends `Access-Control-*` headers to allow other origins. |
| JWT vs sessions? | JWT is stateless and hard to revoke; sessions are server-side and easy to revoke. |
| How to store passwords? | Hash with bcrypt/argon2 (salted, slow); never encrypt or use SHA-256 alone. |
| How to prevent NoSQL injection? | Validate types (strings only), whitelist fields, `sanitizeFilter`, never pass raw `req.body` to queries. |
| Why is Node fast for I/O? | Non-blocking event loop; but CPU-heavy work blocks all requests. |
| How do you scale Express? | Stateless app, multiple processes (PM2/containers), load balancer, Redis for shared state, caching. |
| What is `next('route')`? | Skip the remaining handlers of the current route. |
| How do you structure a project? | Routes -> controllers -> services -> models, config module, central errors. |

### How to answer scenario questions
State the **problem**, the **approach**, the **trade-off** and how you would **test** it. For example: "To protect login from brute force I add a strict rate limit per IP and account, return a generic error, hash with bcrypt, and log failures."

### Coding exercise
Interviewers love asking for a hand-written middleware such as a rate limiter, a logger, or `asyncHandler`. Practise the one in the example: it keeps per-key counters in a Map and answers 429 after the limit.
keyPoints: Explain middleware, order, error handling and the req/res cycle fluently
Security basics: bcrypt, JWT/sessions, CORS, helmet, validation, rate limiting
Be ready to write a small middleware (logger, auth, rate limiter) live
Discuss scaling: stateless design, PM2/containers, Redis, caching
pitfalls: Memorising definitions without being able to show code
Saying "JWT is encrypted" or "CORS protects the server"
Ignoring error paths when writing live code

interview.q: Explain the Express request lifecycle in an interview-ready way.
interview.a: A request enters Express, passes through global middleware in order (security, logging, parsers), reaches the first matching route and its handlers, and ends with a res method; if nothing matches the 404 handler responds, and any thrown or next(err) error is sent to the error-handling middleware.

interview.q: How would you design login security for an Express API?
interview.a: Validate input, hash passwords with bcrypt, return generic errors, rate-limit by IP and account, issue short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, use HTTPS, and log failed attempts.

interview.q: Why is blocking the event loop dangerous?
interview.a: Node runs JavaScript on one thread, so a long synchronous task (huge loops, sync crypto, large JSON parsing) delays every other request; move CPU-heavy work to workers or queues.

interview.q: What is the difference between process.nextTick, setImmediate and a promise callback?
interview.a: nextTick runs before the event loop continues (highest priority), promise callbacks run in the microtask queue right after, and setImmediate runs in the check phase after I/O callbacks.

topics.title: Express vs Fastify vs Koa vs NestJS
topics.summary: Compare the main Node web frameworks by philosophy, speed, features and when each is the right choice.
topics.description:
All four run on Node's `http` module, but they make different trade-offs.

| | Express | Fastify | Koa | NestJS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Style | minimal, callbacks/async | plugin-based, schema-first | minimal, async/await "onion" | opinionated, TypeScript, DI |
| Built-ins | routing, static, few helpers | validation + serialization via JSON Schema, logging (pino) | almost nothing (needs router/body modules) | modules, controllers, guards, pipes, ORM integrations |
| Performance | good | very high (often 2-3x Express in benchmarks) | good | depends on adapter (Express or Fastify) |
| Ecosystem | largest, most tutorials | large and growing | smaller | large, enterprise |
| Learning curve | easiest | easy-moderate | easy | steepest |

### Express
Most popular, huge middleware ecosystem, perfect for learning, MERN and small to mid-size APIs. You design the architecture yourself. Express 5 modernised async handling.

### Fastify
Choose it when throughput and low overhead matter, or when you want built-in validation and fast JSON serialisation from schemas. Plugins are encapsulated, which keeps large codebases tidy. Many Express ideas map directly (routes, hooks instead of middleware).

### Koa
By the Express authors: tiny core, `ctx` object, middleware that can `await next()` and run code before **and** after downstream handlers. Great for those who want a bare toolkit.

### NestJS
Angular-style architecture (modules, decorators, dependency injection) on top of Express or Fastify. Best for large teams and long-lived enterprise apps that need strong conventions and testability. More boilerplate.

### Rule of thumb
Learning, startups, quick APIs: **Express**. Performance-critical or schema-driven services: **Fastify**. Large TypeScript teams: **NestJS**. Minimal custom stacks: **Koa**.
keyPoints: Express: biggest ecosystem and easiest to learn; you choose the architecture
Fastify: fastest, schema validation/serialization built in, plugin encapsulation
Koa: tiny async/await core with an onion middleware model
NestJS: opinionated TypeScript framework with DI that can run on Express or Fastify
Pick by team size, performance needs and need for structure
pitfalls: Choosing a framework only from micro-benchmarks (database and network dominate real latency)
Expecting NestJS to replace Express knowledge (it sits on top of it)

interview.q: When would you choose Fastify over Express?
interview.a: When performance and low overhead matter or you want schema-based validation and serialization out of the box; the trade-off is a smaller ecosystem of drop-in middleware.

interview.q: What is the main difference between Express and Koa middleware?
interview.a: Koa middleware are async functions using await next() so they can run code both before and after downstream handlers (an onion model) and share a ctx object, whereas Express uses (req, res, next) callbacks.

interview.q: Is NestJS a replacement for Express?
interview.a: No. NestJS is a higher-level framework that uses Express (or Fastify) underneath and adds structure such as modules, decorators and dependency injection.

topics.title: Migrating from Express 4 to 5
topics.summary: A checklist of the breaking changes in Express 5 with before/after code and the tools that help.
topics.description:
Express 5 is mostly compatible, but a few changes will break old code. Upgrade steps: use Node 18+, `npm install express@5`, run the codemod, then fix the items below and run your tests.

### Breaking changes checklist
| Area | Express 4 | Express 5 |
|---|---|---|
| Wildcards | `app.get('*', ...)` | `app.get('/*splat', ...)` or `/{*splat}` |
| Optional params | `/:id?` | braces: `/books{/:id}` |
| Inline param regex | `/:id(\d+)` | removed - validate in code |
| Async errors | need `try/catch` + `next(err)` | rejected promises are forwarded automatically |
| `req.query` | writable, parsed with `qs` | getter, parsed by the `simple` parser |
| `req.body` | `{}` when not parsed | `undefined` when not parsed |
| `express.urlencoded` | `extended: true` default | `extended: false` default |
| Removed methods | `app.del()`, `req.param()`, `res.sendfile()` | use `app.delete()`, `req.params/query/body`, `res.sendFile()` |
| `res.json(status, obj)` / `res.send(status)` | worked | **silently sends the number as the body** - use `res.status(n).json(obj)` |
| `res.redirect('back')` | back to referrer | no longer special - use `req.get('Referer') ?? '/'` |
| `res.status(x)` | any value | must be an integer 100-999 |
| `req.host` | hostname only | includes the port (`req.hostname` has none) |
| `app.listen(cb)` | cb ignored errors | cb receives the error (e.g. `EADDRINUSE`) |

### Tooling
`npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade` automates many mechanical edits (check the official migration guide for the current list). Also update middleware packages (`body-parser`, `cookie-parser`, `express-session`, `cors`, `multer`, `express-mongo-sanitize`/`hpp` compatibility) and check each package's changelog for Express 5 support.

### Strategy
Upgrade on a branch, search the code for the patterns above (`'*'`, `.del(`, `res.json(` with two arguments, `req.param(`), run your test suite, then deploy gradually.
keyPoints: Requires Node 18+; run `npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade`
Rename wildcards (`*splat`) and optional params (braces); drop inline regex
Remove v4-only helpers: `app.del`, `req.param`, `res.sendfile`, `res.json(status, body)`
Check body parsing (`req.body` undefined) and `req.query` assumptions
Async handlers no longer need wrappers
pitfalls: `res.send(404)` or `res.json(200, obj)` do NOT fail in v5: they respond 200 with the number as the body
Server crashes at startup with `PathError` because of an old route string
Third-party middleware that mutates `req.query` fails (read-only)

  handler(req, res, next)
})
